# Guideline
## Subject: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR)
## Chapter 1 – Overview of risk-based capital requirements
### Effective Date: November 2023 / January 2024

Note: For institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31 or December 31, respectively.
Subsections 485(1) and 949(1) of the Bank Act (BA), subsection 473(1) of the Trust and Loan Companies Act (TLCA) require banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies to maintain adequate capital. The CAR Guideline is not made pursuant to subsections 485(2) or 949(2) of the BA, or to subsection 473(2) of the TLCA. However, the capital standards set out in this guideline together with the leverage requirements set out in the Leverage Requirements Guideline provide the framework within which the Superintendent assesses whether a bank, a bank holding company, a trust company, or a loan company maintains adequate capital pursuant to the Acts.

For this purpose, the Superintendent has established two minimum standards: the leverage ratio described in the Leverage Requirements Guideline, and the risk-based capital ratio described in this guideline.1 The first test provides an overall measure of the adequacy of an institution's capital. The second measure focuses on risk faced by the institution. Notwithstanding that a bank, bank holding company, trust company, or loan company may meet these standards, the Superintendent may direct a bank or bank holding company to increase its capital under subsections 485(3) or 949(3) of the BA, or a trust company or a loan company to increase its capital under subsection 473(3) of the TLCA.
OSFI, as a member of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, participated in the development of the Basel capital framework on which this guideline is based. Where relevant, the Basel framework paragraph numbers are provided in square brackets at the end of each paragraph referencing material from the Basel framework.

1 The capital and leverage requirements for domestic systemically important banks are supplemented by the requirements described in OSFI's Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) Guideline.
## 1. Purpose and Scope

### 1.1 Purpose
This chapter provides an overview of the risk-based capital requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, collectively referred to as 'institutions'.

### 1.2 Scope
The capital adequacy requirements outlined in this guideline apply on a consolidated basis to all institutions designated by OSFI as domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) and small and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions (SMSBs) which fall into Categories I, II or III as defined in OSFI's SMSB Capital and Liquidity Requirements Guideline.
### 1.3 Effective Date
This guideline is effective as of November 2023 for institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31, and January 2024 for institutions with a fiscal year ending December 31.
# Policy Document Template

## 1. Purpose and Scope

### 1.1 Purpose
This policy outlines the capital adequacy requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies (collectively referred to as 'institutions'). The purpose is to provide a framework for assessing the adequacy of an institution's capital in accordance with the Bank Act and the Trust and Loan Companies Act.
### 1.2 Scope
This policy applies on a consolidated basis to the following institutions:
a. all institutions designated by OSFI as domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs); and
b. small and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions (SMSBs), which fall into Categories I, II or III as defined in OSFI's SMSB Capital and Liquidity Requirements Guideline.

### 1.3 Effective Date
This policy becomes effective in November 2023 for institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31, and in January 2024 for institutions with a fiscal year ending December 31.

## 2. Definitions

D-SIB: Domestic systemically important bank
SMSB: Small and medium-sized deposit-taking institution

## 3. Policy Statement

### 3.1 General Principles
Subsections 485(1) and 949(1) of the Bank Act, and subsection 473(1) of the Trust and Loan Companies Act require institutions to maintain adequate capital. The capital standards set out in this guideline, together with the leverage requirements, provide the framework for the Superintendent to assess capital adequacy.
### 3.2 Specific Requirements

The capital adequacy requirements outlined in this policy are based on the following three risk types:

1. Credit Risk
2. Market Risk
3. Operational Risk

The calculation of risk-weighted assets (RWA) for each of these risk types is described in detail in the subsequent chapters of the Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) guideline.
### 3.3 Exceptions
Notwithstanding that an institution may meet the minimum capital standards, the Superintendent may direct the institution to increase its capital under the applicable provisions of the Bank Act or the Trust and Loan Companies Act.
## 4. Roles and Responsibilities

### 4.1 Management
Management of the institution is responsible for ensuring compliance with the capital adequacy requirements outlined in this policy, including:
- Calculating and monitoring the institution's capital ratios
- Implementing processes and controls to maintain capital at or above the minimum levels
- Escalating any capital shortfalls or exceptions to the Superintendent

### 4.2 Oversight
The Board of Directors is responsible for overseeing the institution's capital management and providing strategic direction to ensure capital adequacy. The Superintendent is responsible for assessing the institution's capital adequacy and taking appropriate supervisory actions.
## 5. Procedures and Controls

### 5.1 Implementation Procedures
Institutions must implement processes to calculate their risk-based capital ratios in accordance with this policy and the detailed requirements set out in the subsequent CAR guideline chapters. This includes:
- Determining the appropriate calculation approach (standardized or internal ratings-based) for credit risk
- Measuring market risk and operational risk exposures
- Aggregating risk-weighted assets and calculating the ratios

### 5.2 Control Mechanisms
Institutions must have robust internal controls and governance processes to ensure the accuracy and integrity of their capital adequacy calculations. This includes:
- Independent validation of models and parameters
- Regular internal and external audits of capital reporting
- Board-level oversight and approval of capital plans

### 5.3 Reporting Requirements
Institutions must report their capital ratios to OSFI on a regular basis, as specified in the CAR guideline. Any breaches of the minimum capital requirements must be promptly escalated to the Superintendent.
## 6. Compliance and Enforcement

### 6.1 Compliance Requirements
Institutions must maintain their capital ratios at or above the minimum levels specified in this policy, including any applicable capital buffers.

### 6.2 Monitoring and Review
OSFI will monitor institutions' compliance with the capital adequacy requirements on an ongoing basis. The policy will be reviewed periodically to ensure it remains aligned with regulatory developments and industry best practices.

### 6.3 Consequences of Non-Compliance
Failure to meet the capital requirements may result in supervisory actions by the Superintendent, including directing the institution to increase its capital levels under the applicable provisions of the Bank Act or the Trust and Loan Companies Act.
## 7. Review and Updates

### 7.1 Review Frequency
This policy will be reviewed by OSFI on an annual basis to ensure it remains current and aligned with regulatory developments.

### 7.2 Update Process
Any changes to this policy will be made through OSFI's standard policy development and consultation process. Affected institutions will be notified of any updates in a timely manner.

### 7.3 Version Control
This is version 1.0 of the Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) policy, effective November 2023/January 2024.
## 8. References
This policy should be read in conjunction with the following related policies, regulations, and standards:
- Bank Act
- Trust and Loan Companies Act
- OSFI Leverage Requirements Guideline
- OSFI Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) Guideline
- Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Framework
## 9. Approval and Authorization

This Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) policy has been approved by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and is effective as of November 2023 for institutions with a fiscal year ending October 31, and January 2024 for institutions with a fiscal year ending December 31.

# Chapter 1 – Overview of Risk-based Capital Requirements

1. Outlined below is an overview of the capital adequacy requirements for banks (including federal credit unions), bank holding companies, federally regulated trust companies, and federally regulated loan companies, collectively referred to as 'institutions'.
2. This chapter is drawn from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) Basel Framework published on the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) website.2 For reference, the Basel paragraph numbers that are associated with the text appearing in this chapter are indicated in square brackets at the end of each paragraph.3
## 1.1. Scope of Application
3. The capital adequacy requirements outlined in this guideline apply on a consolidated basis to the following institutions:
a. all institutions designated by OSFI as domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs); and 
b. small and medium-sized deposit-taking institutions (SMSBs4), which fall into Categories I, II or III as defined in OSFI's SMSB Capital and Liquidity Requirements Guideline.5
## 1.2. Regulatory Capital
5. Total capital consists of the sum of the following elements:
i. Tier 1 capital, consisting of:
a. Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital; and
b. Additional Tier 1 capital
ii. Tier 2 capital
# The criteria for the capital elements comprising the two tiers, as well as the various limits, restrictions and regulatory adjustments to which they are subject, are described in Chapter 2.
## 1.3. Total Risk-weighted Assets
7. Risk-weighted assets (RWA) make up the denominator of the risk-based capital ratios, and is calculated as the higher of:

a. the sum of the following three elements:
  i. RWA for credit risk;
  ii. RWA for market risk; and
  iii. RWA for operational risk; and
b. the adjusted RWA determined as per the capital floor described in section 1.5.
[Basel Framework, RBC 20.4]
### 1.3.1. Credit Risk
8. RWA for credit risk (including counterparty credit risk) is calculated as the sum of:
a. Credit RWA for banking book exposures which, except the RWA listed in (b) through (e) below, is calculated using:
  i. the standardized approach (as set out in Chapter 4); or
  ii. the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approach (as set out in Chapter 5).
b. RWA for counterparty credit risk from banking book exposures and trading book exposures (as set out in Chapter 7), except the exposures listed in (c) and (f) below.
c. Credit RWA for equity investments in funds that are held in the banking book calculated using one or more of the approaches set out in Chapter 4:
  i. The look-through approach
  ii. The mandate-based approach
  iii. The fall-back approach
d. RWA for securitization exposures held in the banking book, calculating using one or more of the approaches set out in Chapter 6:
  i. Securitization Standardized Approach (SEC-SA)
  ii. Securitization External Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-ERBA)
  iii. Securitization Internal Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-IRBA)
  iv. Securitization Internal Assessment Approach (SEC-IAA)
  v. A risk weight of 1250% in cases where the institution cannot use (i) to (iv) above.
